get.summary: Fetch normalized transactions for a connection
get.description:
Transactions are fetched live from the bank on each call and never stored, so this is a pull API. Sync contract for keeping your own system up to date: on the first pull omit the date filters; on each later pull pass since=<the next_cursor from your previous response> to fetch only from where you left off. The response always returns next_cursor (the end of the window just fetched). Poll on your own cadence and use it as the next since. Because the boundary day can overlap, deduplicate by each transaction's id.

**The first pull gets all the history the bank will give.** The first call on a connection without dates asks the bank for every transaction it will provide, and the response carries `history: "all"`. Banks differ: many give a year or more, but mostly only shortly after the account holder connects, and after that many give only 90 days. So make that first call soon after the connection activates. Be ready for it to return years of transactions, to take longer than a normal pull, and to use extra calls at the bank. Every later call without dates returns the last 90 days, unless the all-history answer came back `truncated`: that does not count as the first pull, so the next call without dates asks for all history again. To choose instead, send `history=recent` for the last 90 days (the first pull included) or `history=all` to ask for all history again. With `?enrich=true`, an all-history pull enriches only the last 90 days unless you also send `enrich_history=all`; older rows come back with `enrichment_skipped: true` and are not charged.

**Every call with `enrich=true` is billed, including rows already enriched.** With a live key, each call counts every transaction it returns toward your enrichment usage, your free monthly allowance first and then your prepaid balance, including transactions an earlier call already enriched. Only rows marked `enrichment_skipped` or `enrichment_pending` are not counted. So store what you receive and fetch only new transactions with `since`, rather than fetching the same window again.

**How often to poll.** A pull reuses the connection's existing bank session, so it does not consume a new Active Session, and the pull itself is not metered (enrichment is, as above). The limit that binds is the PSD2 one: RTS (EU) 2018/389 Art. 36(5)(b) allows an account information service no more than four unattended accesses in a 24-hour period, unless a higher frequency is agreed with the bank, with your user's consent. We enforce it for you: 4 unattended fetches per connection per UTC day, after which this endpoint answers 429 with a `resets_at`. A fetch that fails at the bank still counts. That is not a limit on your account, and stopping at it is what keeps the connection working for you and for everyone else on the platform. A fetch made while your own user is on screen is exempt under Art. 36(5)(a) and does not count. Polling harder does not get you data sooner either: a payment visible in the bank's own app is not necessarily booked over PSD2 yet, and until it is, no number of calls will return it.

**When the bank is down.** After a fetch for a connection times out at the bank or gets a server error, automated fetches for that connection are paused for five minutes: this endpoint answers 503 `bank_unavailable` at once, with a `Retry-After`, without contacting the bank or using a fetch from the allowance. So retrying into an outage does not use up the day. A fetch made while your user is on screen is not paused.

**Required scope:** `connect:read`.

parameters.name: account_id
parameters.description: EB account uid; omit to fetch all accounts on the connection.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Incremental cursor: the next_cursor from your previous response. Sets the window start when date_from is not given. Dedupe by transaction id across the boundary.

parameters.name: date_from
parameters.description: Explicit window start (overrides since).

parameters.name: history
parameters.description: Which range a pull without dates reads. `all`: every transaction the bank will give, which may be years, slower, and use extra bank calls. `recent`: the last 90 days. When omitted, the first pull on a connection is `all` and every later one is `recent`. Cannot be combined with date_from or since; `all` cannot be combined with a date_to before today.

parameters.name: enrich
parameters.description: Run enrichment on each transaction (needs enrichment:read). Billed on every call: with a live key, each returned transaction counts toward your enrichment usage, including transactions an earlier call already enriched, except rows marked `enrichment_skipped` or `enrichment_pending`. Store the results on your side rather than fetching the same window again. Enrichment may send transactions to our AI provider; see POST /v1/enrich.

parameters.name: enrich_history
parameters.description: With enrich=true on an all-history pull: `recent` (the default) enriches only the last 90 days and marks older rows `enrichment_skipped`, uncharged; `all` enriches and charges for every row. Other pulls enrich every row either way. Needs enrich=true.

parameters.name: underwrite
parameters.description: Run the full underwriting analysis (enrichment always included; bills the per-applicant underwriting meter; needs underwriting:write). Returns the analysis bundle instead of transactions.

parameters.name: psu-ip-address
parameters.description: The IP address of your end user, when one is actively waiting on this call. Send with `Psu-User-Agent`; either both or neither. Never your own server's address.

parameters.name: psu-user-agent
parameters.description: The User-Agent of your end user's browser. Send with `Psu-Ip-Address`; either both or neither.

date_from.description: The start of the window read. On an all-history pull, the earliest booking date the bank returned, or null when it returned nothing.

history.description: Present only when this pull asked the bank for all the history it will give, as the first pull without dates does. Absent means a dated or 90-day window.

enriched_from.description: With enrich=true. Rows booked before this date were not enriched or charged and carry `enrichment_skipped: true`. Null when every row was eligible.

enrichment_skipped_count.description: With enrich=true. How many rows were deliberately not enriched because they fall before `enriched_from`. Not pending: calling again does not enrich them. Send enrich_history=all for that.

accounts_fetched.description: How many accounts on this connection this answer covers. The account list is the one recorded when the holder authorised the connection, so if you know the connection has more accounts than this, the missing one never reached us and needs re-authorising.

truncated.description: Present only when the answer is partial: we stopped paginating at our own page ceiling rather than because the bank ran out, so there are more transactions in this window than are returned here. The ceiling applies to each account separately; `truncated_accounts` names the ones that hit it, and the other accounts are complete. Narrow the window with `date_from` / `date_to` and fetch again. Absent means complete. A truncated pull without dates does not use up the first pull: the next pull without dates asks for all history again.

truncated_accounts.description: Present with `truncated`: the `account_id` of each account whose transactions were cut off at the page ceiling. Every other account in this answer is complete for the window.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `since` on your next pull. The end of the window just fetched, so the boundary day can overlap: deduplicate by transaction id.

account_id.description: Which account on this connection the entry belongs to, matching `account_id` from the accounts endpoint. Always present: every entry is fetched for one account and tagged with it.

id.description: The bank's own reference for this entry: `entry_reference` when the bank sends one, else `transaction_id`. Safe to deduplicate on only when `id_source` is `entry_reference`; otherwise match on `date`, `amount` and `descriptor`.

id_source.description: Which field `id` came from. `entry_reference` is unique and stable for the account. `transaction_id` is not: Enable Banking notes it may change when the list is fetched again. Null when the bank sent neither.

entry_reference.description: The bank's unique, stable reference for the entry on this account, as sent. Not unique across accounts.

transaction_id.description: The identifier the bank uses for fetching entry details, as sent. Not a stable reference.

date.description: YYYY-MM-DD. The booking date; where the bank sends none, the value date, and failing that the transaction date. Null only when the bank sends none of the three. A booked entry can appear a day or more after the money moved: a weekend credit is commonly visible in the bank's own app before it is booked over PSD2, and until it is booked no amount of polling returns it.

booking_date.description: YYYY-MM-DD. The date the bank booked the entry, when it sends one.

value_date.description: YYYY-MM-DD. The date the money became available (credit) or stopped being available (debit), when the bank sends one.

transaction_date.description: YYYY-MM-DD. The card transaction date, or the date the bank received a transfer or direct debit, when the bank sends one. Some banks send only this date.

amount.description: The decimal amount Enable Banking reports, in the currency's major unit and never rescaled: EUR 22.40 is `22.4`, never `2240`. How many decimal places a bank sends varies by currency. Signed from `credit_debit`: negative is money out (`DBIT`), positive is money in (`CRDT`). Enable Banking requires the indicator on every entry; if one were ever missing, `credit_debit` is null and this is the unsigned amount, so treat its direction as unknown. Null when the bank sends no amount, or one that does not start with a number.

currency.description: ISO 4217 code. Null only when the bank sends none.

descriptor.description: Raw text we enrich from: the counterparty name, else the remittance text. Because the name wins, the payment communication is usually not here; read `remittance_information` and `structured_reference` for that.

counterparty_name.description: Null on entries where the bank sends no counterparty. Some banks omit it on a large share of entries, in which case there is no text to identify a merchant from and enrichment returns nothing for that row.

counterparty_iban.description: The other party's IBAN: the payer on money in, the payee on money out. Null when the bank does not send it; some banks send a domestic account number instead (see `counterparty_bban`).

counterparty_bban.description: The other party's domestic account number (BBAN), when the bank sends that instead of an IBAN. Same direction rule as `counterparty_iban`.

remittance_information.description: The payment communication lines exactly as the bank sent them: free text, a structured reference, or both. Empty when the bank sent none.

reference_number.description: A creditor reference the bank has labelled as such, as sent. Many banks leave it empty and put the reference in `remittance_information`.

reference_number_scheme.description: The scheme the bank gives for `reference_number`, as sent: for example `BERF` (Belgian structured reference) or `INTL` (ISO 11649, starting RF).

structured_reference.description: A structured payment reference whose check digits are valid, for matching a payment to an invoice. Taken from `reference_number` when the bank labels one, otherwise found in `remittance_information`. Null when there is none, when its check digits fail, or when the communication carries two different references.

scheme.description: `BE`: Belgian structured communication (OGM/VCS). `RF`: ISO 11649 creditor reference.

reference.description: Compact form: 12 digits for `BE`, uppercase with no spaces for `RF`.

formatted.description: As printed on an invoice, for example `+++090/9337/55493+++`.

status.description: The entry's status as Enable Banking reports it: `BOOK` (booked), `PDNG` (pending), `CNCL` (cancelled), `HOLD` (account hold), `RJCT` (rejected), `SCHD` (scheduled) or `OTHR` (unknown). Only `BOOK` means booked, so post to a ledger on `BOOK` alone. Enable Banking requires a status on every entry; if one were ever missing this is null, which is not booked either.

pending.description: Exactly `status === "PDNG"`, so the two never disagree. We do not ask the bank for pending entries, so this reflects only what a bank volunteers and is false on most connections. `false` means "not marked pending", not "booked": a cancelled, rejected, held or scheduled entry is also `false`. Use `status` to decide whether an entry is booked.

bank_code_description.description: The bank's own label for what kind of transaction this is. Available on some banks only.

bank_code_codes.description: The bank's transaction type codes as sent (ISO 20022 or proprietary). Empty when the bank sends none.

bank_code_iso_pair.description: The ISO 20022 family and sub-family, when the bank sends them. Null when it sends only a domain or nothing.

enrichment_skipped.description: With enrich=true on an all-history pull: this row is older than `enriched_from`, so it was not enriched and not charged. Send enrich_history=all to enrich it.

post.summary: Mint a disconnect link for the account holder
post.description:
A short-lived URL that ends this one connection and nothing else, usable without an API key.

Put it behind a Disconnect control in your own product so the person whose bank account it is can withdraw without going through you, and without your front end holding a Distyra key. Under Model 3 that person has no Distyra account and we hold no contact details for them, so you are the only one who can put this in front of them.

**The URL is the capability.** Anyone holding it can end this one connection, so treat it like a password reset link: mint it when you render the control, do not log it, and do not email it. It expires, and revoking is idempotent.

Your front end sends `POST` to the URL. A `GET` does nothing, deliberately: a link checker or a browser prefetch must not be able to disconnect a customer's bank.

**Required scope:** `connect:write`.

parameters.name: expires_in_hours
parameters.description: How long the link stays usable. Defaults to 72 hours, capped at 7 days.

post.summary: Mint a hosted bank-connect link for an account holder
post.description:
Returns a URL you send to whoever is connecting the account. Opening it starts the hosted pick-a-bank and consent flow, so you never handle bank credentials.

Set `mode` to say whose account it is. For a product whose customers each connect their own bank (an accounting or bookkeeping SaaS, for example), that is `mode: 'end_user'` with your own `external_ref` to identify the customer and a `return_url` to land them back in your app. That combination needs no Underwriting subscription.

`mode` and `applicant_ref` must agree: `applicant_ref` on its own still means an underwriting applicant, and sending it alongside a different `mode` is refused rather than guessed at. Omitting `mode` keeps the old inference, which resolves to `own` when no `applicant_ref` is present.

The page shows the name, accent colour and logo your organization sets under Connect branding in the portal. `brand_name` and `brand_color` override the first two for one link. The logo is the image you upload there, served from our own servers so the account holder's browser contacts no other site. It cannot be set per link: a request that sends `brand_logo_url` is refused with `brand_logo_url_unsupported`.

external_ref.description:
Your own stable id for the connection this link creates. Survives reconsent; echoed in list responses and every connect.connection.* webhook.

Use a pseudonymous id, meaningful only inside your own systems. Do not put a name, email address or other directly identifying detail here: we cannot tell one from the other, we store what you send, and you are the controller for it. We erase it when your organization is deleted, and billing records reference the connection rather than this value so the erasure holds.

**Required scope:** `connect:write`.

mode.description: Whose account the link is for. Same rules as POST /v1/connect/connections: omit and we infer from applicant_ref, send `end_user` for a user of your own application. Signed into the link, so the connection it creates carries the mode you asked for. If a mode is not available for your organization, the request is refused with `connect_mode_unavailable`. When business verification is required, a live `end_user` link is checked when it is minted and again when it is used.

brand_name.description: Override the hosted page brand name for this link (defaults to your org branding).

brand_color.description: Override brand accent colour (#RRGGBB) for this link.

psu_type.description: Whether the account to connect is a business or a personal one. The hosted page opens with this choice and lists the banks that offer that type of account; the account holder can change it there, since they are the one who knows. Defaults to `business`.

expires_in_hours.description:
How long the link stays usable, in hours. Defaults to 72, capped at 7 days.

This bounds when the account holder may **start**, not when they may finish. Once they have chosen their bank, the flow runs on that bank's clock, and an authorization begun just before the link expired will still activate the connection when it completes. So do not treat `expires_at` as the moment an attempt dies: to clean up attempts that never finished, measure age from the connection's own `created_at` (which is when the authorization began) and send `expected_status=pending` on the delete.

post.summary: Rotate the current API key with a 14-day overlap
post.description: Creates a new API key and marks the current key for expiry in 14 days. The new key inherits the current key's scopes. Both keys remain valid until the current key's `expires_at` passes, giving caller infrastructure a window to roll over without downtime. The raw new key value is returned exactly once, so store it immediately. No recovery mechanism exists; if the response is lost, rotate again.

scope.description: 429 only. Which window tripped: `burst` (per-second) or `sustained` (per-minute average).

retry_after_seconds.description: On a 429, and on a 503 `bank_unavailable` from Connect. Seconds to wait before retrying. Mirrors the `Retry-After` header for clients that would rather not parse headers.

max.description: 429 only. The limit that was exceeded, in the units of `scope` (requests/second for `burst`, requests/minute for `sustained`).

tags.name: connect
tags.description:
Live PSD2/AIS bank connections (Distyra Connect). Fetch normalized transactions from a bank account on demand. Nothing is stored.

`mode` says whose account it is: `own` (your organization’s), `end_user` (a customer of your product, for anyone embedding Connect in something they sell), or `applicant` (an underwriting applicant). Only `applicant` needs an Underwriting subscription. Billed per active connection per month.

### Connecting a bank account, start to finish

**1. Ask for a link.** `POST /v1/connect/hosted-link` with the bank’s two-letter country code, e.g. `{ "country": "NL" }`. For a customer’s account also send `mode: "end_user"`, your own `external_ref` to identify them, and a `return_url`. Returns `{ url, token, expires_at }`.

**2. Send the account holder to that `url`.** They pick their bank and log in on the bank’s own site. Neither you nor we see their credentials. The bank returns them to your `return_url`.

**3. Wait to be told it worked.** Listen for `connect.connection.activated`, or poll `GET /v1/connect/connections` for one with `status` `active`. Do not treat the `return_url` redirect as success: they may have cancelled.

**4. See what you got.** `GET /v1/connect/connections/{id}/accounts`. One consent often covers several accounts.

**5. Fetch transactions.** `GET /v1/connect/connections/{id}/transactions`. First call: no dates, and you get all the history the bank will give, which can be years; make it soon after the connection activates, because many banks give long history only then. Every later call without dates gives 90 days. After the first call pass `since=` the previous response’s `next_cursor`, and de-duplicate on transaction `id` because the boundary day can overlap. `history=recent` limits any call, the first included, to 90 days. `?enrich=true` adds merchant names, logos and categories. Every call fetches from the bank, so poll on the schedule your product needs rather than in a loop.

**6. Let them disconnect.** `POST /v1/connect/connections/{id}/revoke-link` returns a short-lived, keyless URL to put behind a Disconnect button. `DELETE /v1/connect/connections/{id}` does the same from your backend.

**Consent expires** on a date set by the account holder’s bank, and banks differ. Each connection’s `consent_expires_at` gives the exact date, and `max_consent_days` on `GET /v1/connect/aspsps` gives a bank’s limit before anyone connects. If you need one number to plan around, use 90 days: no bank we connect to allows less. An `applicant` connection closes after 7 days. For `own` and `end_user` you get `connect.connection.reconsent_required` before it lapses, and every connection sends `connect.connection.expired` after. Reconnect by repeating step 1 with the same `external_ref`, which is what keeps your records pointing at the right customer.
